lines: 1011 lines of Markdown. Prose is wrapped at about 76 columns, so the count runs past the 500 to 900 expected. Tables and the two defect lists account for most of the excess.
outline: Status line: a record in progress dated 2026-11-15; 13 of 20 languages ported; 3 measurements running; the working files are not in this repository; the roles named; 'ran' and 'read' defined

1. What was tested. 1.1 the proposal in its restated form, with what is shared and what a language supplies (naming hook; syntax provider of printers, declared facts and notes; the forms the guard reads). 1.2 the three sections and the twenty languages. 1.3 H1 to H5 as a table, verbatim from the brief

2. How it was tested. 2.1 a table of the ten stages. 2.2 the rule each round added and the finding that forced it, plus the table pairing each kind of fact with its kind of check. 2.3 what 'ported' means. 2.4 the environment, stated as a fact about that machine

3. Results so far, hypothesis by hypothesis. 3.1 H1, each of its three criteria separately. 3.2 H2: the 3.2 table, the projection, the history of the figure, and why the per-port ratios are not H2's measure. 3.3 H3: not measured. 3.4 H4: lane table and the unverified blocks. 3.5 H5: stages 1 and 2 only

4. What the build found that the proposal did not say. 4.1 a shared sentence is a claim about twenty runtimes. 4.2 a declared fact needs a check. 4.3 'the same sentence' must be defined before a sentence can be reviewed once. 4.4 the comparison with the old page is a reading aid, not a check. 4.5 (added) per-language content is not all syntax. 4.6 (added) porting one section at a time makes documents contradict each other. 4.7 runtime defects, one line each. 4.8 defects of main's pages and tests, one line each

5. What it cost. 5.1 interface changes by round (breaking, additive, cause, how many came from a newly ported language). 5.2 review labour. 5.3 the review tools and their self-test. 5.4 one port in the first wave
Appendix A. The thirteen languages at 3.3, one row each, plus the guard account
Appendix B. Interface changes: breaking changes one row each (34 rows); additive changes counted per round
Appendix C. Attacks that nothing mechanical catches at 3.3
outline_changes: Added 4.5 'Per-language content is not all syntax' (the analysis of the other ten README families). It bears on how far the result generalises, and none of the outline's examples covered it.
Added 4.6 'Porting one section at a time makes documents contradict each other', a finding repeated from stage 1 to 3.3.

H1 in 3.1 is reported criterion by criterion, because its three refutation criteria stand differently: model reads hold, prose is under the line by one measure and over it by another, and the breaking-change count is crossed.

Appendix B lists the breaking changes one row each and counts the additive ones per round in 5.1, without a row each. There are more than seventy additive changes, and listing them would bury the breaking ones. The appendix says that it departs from the outline.
Section 2.1 numbers the stages 1 to 10 so later sections can refer to them; the version numbers 3.1, 3.2 and 3.3 are defined before they are used.
unanswered: Would a maintainer adopt this for three sections only? The records hold no measure of a partial adoption: the three ported sections alongside the ten unported README families. The only evidence is the contradictions this created (section 4.6).

What does the review machinery cost to maintain once the porting is done? The records give self-test sizes and times, and the 40 and 16 controls that had to be re-aimed after text changes. They say nothing about steady-state cost, or about which tools would ship in the repository and which would stay prototype scaffolding.

Which parts of the guard and the review tools would be committed to sdkgen? None of the records proposes a shipping form. The H2 counts that include the guard therefore assume a cost whose final size is unknown.
Does the approach hold for real specifications rather than the one Demo model and its 21 variations? No run used a real API's model.

Will the seven remaining languages (js, php, csharp, java, kotlin, scala, cpp) need new breaking changes? Unknown until they are ported. The 3.3 round showed that new languages' reviews do cause them.
What H3 is against the 329-issue catalogue, and what H5 is on the current structure: both are running.
Whether the separate tools branch built beside the 3.3 freeze (225a0de) was merged into the frozen tools. The records say it was not, as of the freeze.

How many readers the stage-9 survey had: brief 7 and the survey's own header say ten readers, two runtimes each. The short form does not say, so one digest called it unknown. The record states ten, from the survey header.
Elapsed wall-clock time per stage. Only the first-wave ports and the rb pilot record times; the other stages do not.
disagreements: H1 breaking-change count over the same span. Version 2 counted 4; the stage-3 builder and its checker counted about 6, because they classify the naming hook (Ent.sym) differently. Written: both counts, with the naming hook marked as disputed in Appendix B.

Breaking changes at version 3. The builder counted about 11, then about 12 at the freeze; the checker counted about 10 from type diffs. Written: all three figures, attributed. Later records use about 11 to 13 at 3.1.

Which three shared changes were breaking at 3.3. The shared builder named decisions 12, 13 and 14; the freezing builder named streamSignal, the wrapped unwrap and the utility copy, and called arity additive. Written: the freezing builder's classification, which the 25 to 27 count rests on, with the disagreement stated in 5.1.

Whether newly ported languages caused breaking changes. The 3.1 and 3.2 builders and the first-wave porters said none; brief 7 said no port needed one. The 3.3 freeze says 2 or 3 of that round's breaking changes answered the first-wave reviews. Written: none up to 3.2 and none while porting, then 2 or 3 at 3.3.

H1 prose verdict. The 3.1 checker judged it refuted (go 25.6%, go-only words plus notes); the 3.1 builder judged it 'partly'. The 3.2 measure gives go 22.6% alone and 7.4% by source; the stage-9 verifier gives 18.6% alone and showed that only 9 of 77 single-language sentences are a runtime's own fact. Written: both measures, defined. The record does not call the criterion crossed by source, and says the 'alone' measure crosses it for go.

go notes on the version-3 REFERENCE. The builder measured 20.5%, then 20.4%; the checker measured 18.9% with a different denominator. Not quoted as current, since these figures were superseded at 3.1 and 3.2.

H2 at 3.1. The builder gave 1.65x measured and 2.30x projected for documentation code; the tools' headline gave 1.34x and 1.75x. Written in the H2 history. The 3.2 figures (1.61x, 1.33x, 0.98x, tool headline 1.29x) are given as current and say what each counts.

The first-wave digest says that with forms every port except ocaml is at or above 3.1x, 'above H2's 2x threshold'. Written: per-port ratios without forms from the 3.3 numstat (perl 3.3x, swift 3.7x, ocaml 2.7x, lua 3.9x), with the statement that these exclude shared code and are not H2's measure.

Time per port. Brief 7 said 'about half an hour' each. The records give perl and lua 30 minutes (lua's clock doubted by its porter), and swift and ocaml from 02:01 to about 04:15. Written: the records' times; 'half an hour' fits provider-and-hook writing, not a whole port.

The 3.2 guard and stream disagreements: clojure and elixir streamLazy were called WRONG by the guard engineer and kept, with corrected sentences, by the shared engineer; ocaml's stream kind is unresolved. Written: the stream sentence findings in 4.1, and ocaml's stream kind under Not done.

Hand record f64ae2f4fc (log's default). The ocaml reviewer called its reason false, while the lua reviewer judged the same id right for lua. Not written as a line, since no record settles it; it falls under 'hand records found wrong' in 4.4.

The guard engineer's list of match-getter copy citations (8 languages) left out c, clojure and zig; the shared engineer and the freeze found they clone too. Written implicitly: 4.2 notes that the guard had omissions, closed when found.

Whether a dropped go or c branch sentence leaves a trace. The first half of the 3.3 freeze said it leaves none in either mode; the tools round measured that at 6e224b8 it was already an absent entry in both modes, and only the one-variation drop from scratch was open. Written: the frozen state, in Appendix C, as a sentence only go's style prints, dropped from scratch (a moved control).
The unported pages' diff against OLD: 7 and 8 lines at 3.2, 6 and 7 at 3.3, not reconciled. Written: only that the seven unported pages are byte-identical to the 3.2 output.
summary:
I wrote the record of the prototype for the repository's maintainers. It covers the proposal, the refutation criteria as fixed in advance, ten stages of building and independent checking, results hypothesis by hypothesis, what the build found that the proposal did not say, the cost, limits, outstanding work, and three appendices.

**H2 is refuted.** At 3.2, the last full measurement, the nine measured languages shrank by these ratios:
- 1.61x counting documentation code only;
- 1.33x adding the forms the guard reads;
- 0.98x adding the shared guard;
- 1.29x by the tools' own headline count.

The only figure above 2x is documentation code alone, projected to twenty languages at the measured provider size: 2.26x.

**H1 is refuted on the breaking-change criterion.** The count is about 25 to 27 at 3.3, against a limit of about 10. It was first reached at version 3, with none caused by a newly ported language through 3.2, and 2 or 3 at 3.3. The record also states what the criterion does not measure. H1 holds on model reads: 0 open in all 13 languages. On prose, it is under 15% measured by source (highest go, 7.4%), but over 15% for go by the 'printed alone' measure (18.6%). The record shows that measure mostly counts shared code that one condition selects.

**H3 and H5 are not measured on the current structure.** H3 has never been measured against the catalogue, and both measurements are running.

**H4 holds where a toolchain exists.** The lanes pass for ts, go, py, c, rust, rb, zig and perl, and two lanes that failed on old code are now fixed. It is untested for clojure, elixir, swift, ocaml and lua. The perl root-import regression was found and fixed with an additive change.

Sections 4.7 and 4.8 list the runtime defects and the defects of main's pages and tests, one line each with a file where one is given. No temporary paths or model names appear in the document.
